lesson.title: Union: Combining Sets Without Duplicates
lesson.summary: Union merges every element from two or more sets into one new set, automatically dropping duplicates, and Python offers two ways to write it: the | operator between sets and the more flexible .union() method.
lesson.body:
Set Operations covered intersection, difference, and symmetric difference, all of which compare two sets against each other. Union is different: instead of comparing, it combines. The union of two sets is a brand new set containing every element that appears in either one, with duplicates automatically collapsed down to a single copy, exactly the way any set behaves.

weekday_readers = {"Ana", "Ben", "Cleo"}
weekend_readers = {"Cleo", "Dev"}

all_readers = weekday_readers | weekend_readers
print(sorted(all_readers))

book_club = weekday_readers.union(weekend_readers, {"Eli"})
print(sorted(book_club))

The | operator prints ['Ana', 'Ben', 'Cleo', 'Dev']: Cleo appears in both original sets but shows up only once in the union, since a set can never hold duplicates. The .union() method does the same job as | but can accept more than one set at a time, so book_club combines three sets in a single call and prints ['Ana', 'Ben', 'Cleo', 'Dev', 'Eli'].

The two spellings are not perfectly interchangeable, though, and the difference is worth knowing before it surprises you. The .union() method is willing to accept any iterable at all, not just another set, and will pull elements out of it. The | operator is stricter and only works between two actual sets.

more_readers = weekday_readers.union(["Frank", "Ana"])
print(sorted(more_readers))

try:
    weekday_readers | ["Frank"]
except TypeError as e:
    print("Error:", e)

print(sorted(weekday_readers))

The first print shows ['Ana', 'Ben', 'Cleo', 'Frank']: .union() happily accepted a plain list, pulled "Frank" and "Ana" out of it, and merged them in, again dropping the repeated "Ana". The try block prints Error: unsupported operand type(s) for |: 'set' and 'list', because | refuses to combine a set with anything that is not also a set. The final print shows ['Ana', 'Ben', 'Cleo'], the original weekday_readers completely unchanged, which is true of every example in this lesson: union, whichever way you write it, always builds and returns a new set rather than modifying either of the sets you started with.
